title: Hijack Execution Flow: KernelCallbackTable
summary: This sub-technique hijacks a graphical process from inside by rewriting one entry of its KernelCallbackTable, a structure in the PEB that user32.dll fills with the callback routines Windows calls when it delivers certain messages. The table sits in user-mode memory, so an adversary with write access to the target process can point an entry such as fnCOPYDATA at a payload, then trigger the callback by sending the process an ordinary window message. The pointer is located by reading the PEB, for example through a native query call, and the replacement is written with a memory write call, sometimes after copying the table so the original layout is preserved. Execution then appears to originate from the legitimate process rather than a newly created one, and the payload may restore the original entry afterwards. Detection is behavioural: memory scanning or instrumentation for code inside a process image that does not match the file on disk, the calling thread being the messaging thread, and network or file activity attributed to a GUI process that never normally performs it. This differs from sibling hijacks in that no service, path, or .NET setting is touched; only live process memory changes.

beginner.definition: Graphical Windows programs keep a small list of helper functions in memory. Windows calls one of these helpers when the program receives a message, such as a copy request. An attacker who can write into that program memory can replace one helper with their own code. The program then runs attacker code while it looks normal.
beginner.whyItMatters: The malicious code runs inside a trusted program, so it inherits that program trust and identity. Security tools that watch for new or unusual programs may see nothing unusual. It can also be used to hide activity or to reach data the program can read. The victim process usually keeps working, so users notice nothing wrong.
howItWorks: A graphical program loads the user interface library and receives a table of callbacks.
The table lives in the program memory and holds addresses of helper functions.
An attacker obtains write access to that memory, often through another injection step.
They copy the table, then change one entry to point at their own code.
A normal window message is sent to the program to trigger that entry.
Attacker code runs as part of the program, which may restore the table afterwards.
beginner.example: Picture an office with a printed list of phone numbers for each task, such as calling the courier. Someone swaps one number on the list for their own. A clerk dials the same line on the list as always, but reaches the stranger instead. Nothing about the office routine changed, so nobody suspects the list.
takeaways: Trust in a process does not mean the code inside it is trustworthy.
Compare memory code against the file on disk to find hidden payloads.
Treat network or file actions by graphical programs as worth checking.

objectives: Explain what the KernelCallbackTable is and where it lives in a process.
Describe how a single table entry can be redirected to attacker code.
State why this execution can appear to come from a legitimate process.
Identify memory and behaviour evidence used to detect this technique.
Compare this hijack with other execution flow hijacking methods.
